speaker: John
line: In Transformer Architectures, today’s lecture is on Triadic Linear Attention. Long-context research is exploring several ways to remember more without keeping every token in a growing cache. Titans adds a learned long-term memory, while Mixture-of-Memories uses multiple recurrent states. This paper takes a different route: it gives a recurrent state another address axis. That matters because a fixed-state model can be efficient, but may have trouble recalling details from far back in a book. Go ahead, Noah.

speaker: Noah
line: Hi Professor, how does that extra address axis help a recurrent model remember more?

speaker: John
line: Think of a recurrent model reading the final pages of a long book. It must carry useful details forward in a fixed-size state, whereas a Transformer can retain a growing key-value cache, using more memory as context expands. Triadic attention stores each value under two learned addresses rather than one. That enlarges the recurrent memory while avoiding a proportional expansion of the sequence-mixer projections. The added capacity is useful, but it is not free or unlimited.

speaker: John
line: In ordinary linear attention, each token writes a key-value association into a matrix state, and a later query reads from that state. The triadic version also produces a second key and a second query. It binds the value to both keys, so the state has an additional axis. The model can then use both queries to retrieve the stored value. In effect, it can distinguish more associations within a recurrent memory.

speaker: Noah
line: So the second address makes the state larger, but does it also make every part of the model larger?

speaker: John
line: The state grows by a factor set by E, the number of slices along that added axis. The main construction adds projections for the second key and query, but does not widen every sequence-mixer projection to the same degree. In the language models, those paths also use a short convolution and a softplus activation, and each state slice has its own forget gate. For Gated DeltaNet, the update erases an old association before writing its corrected value.

speaker: John
line: The authors first isolate memory capacity with a deliberately small key-value retrieval task. A model stores associations, then sees their keys in random order and must return the matching values. As E increases, accuracy holds up with more stored pairs. At E of 16, the authors report roughly 16 times as many associations as ordinary linear attention, with just 1.08 times the non-embedding parameters. That result describes this controlled task, not a general guarantee for language models.

speaker: Noah
line: How do they make such a larger state practical to train on a GPU?

speaker: John
line: They derive a chunkwise-parallel training method, allowing computation over blocks rather than relying only on token-by-token recurrence. They also tile the state along its value axis, so one GPU processing unit does not have to hold the entire third-order state at once. These choices make training feasible, but do not turn the approach into a faster inference method. The paper reports about 28 to 30% training overhead for E of 8 over vanilla Gated DeltaNet.

speaker: John
line: For language modeling, the authors test on held-out P-G-19 books and evaluate next-token prediction across contexts extended up to 64,000 tokens. Their reported comparison shows Triadic Gated DeltaNet with E of 8 predicting better than the Transformer even at 64,000 tokens. They also evaluate recall across six tasks, where an answer counts as correct if the generated text contains it. Those results address retrieval separately from book-text prediction.

speaker: Noah
line: What is the most convincing comparison for showing that the extra address, rather than simply more state, helps?

speaker: John
line: The key comparison matches state size and nearly matches parameter budgets. At 400 million model parameters and four times the state, Triadic Gated DeltaNet has a 25.2 megabyte state and a six-task Recall average of 31.1. The strongest listed Gated DeltaNet alternative, larger heads, has the same stated state size and scores 28.5. The reported scores average three seeds; the parameter totals are close, not identical.

speaker: John
line: The authors also report lower perplexity for triadic Gated DeltaNet than each state-enlargement alternative across all three P-G-19 context ranges. Their analysis suggests the added state is used to retain information across different timescales: the slices have varied measured half-lives, and the model benefits from more distant context. These observations support their interpretation, but do not establish that the extra axis alone causes every performance difference.

speaker: Noah
line: Does that mean the approach settles the tradeoff between recall and memory cost?

speaker: John
line: No. It makes a fixed recurrent state roomier, but the state still occupies memory, and its capacity remains finite. The findings are also specific to the tested Gated DeltaNet and scalar-gated linear attention models. This connects to the broader direction represented by Titans and Mixture-of-Memories: researchers are changing how models retain history, rather than assuming a Transformer cache is the only option. Triadic attention contributes a particular way to allocate recurrent memory.

speaker: John
line: The practical takeaway is to distinguish memory capacity from memory cost. A second learned address can improve recall and long-context prediction under the tested conditions, and the model’s recurrent state remains fixed in size as the sequence grows. But enlarging that state costs memory and adds training overhead; the paper does not claim cheaper end-to-end inference. When you evaluate recurrent memory designs, ask not only how much they retain, but how effectively they use each added state entry. Thanks for listening.
